title: Weak D, Partial D and DEL: Find It in Donors, Protect Patients
summary: Tell weak D (less D), partial D (missing epitopes) and DEL (traces only) apart, and apply the opposite donor and patient rules, including RHD genotyping for serological weak D.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 40 Hits 12 and 16 (partial D makes anti-D; weak D types 1/2/3 managed as D-positive; RHD genotyping), Hit 17 (DEL detectable only by adsorption–elution; DEL units can immunize) and Trap 3 (donor vs recipient rules). Checked against Sandler 2015 (AABB/CAP Work Group), Sandler 2017, Suksard 2024 and Sainath 2025. Added context: Asian-type DEL patients may tolerate D-positive blood; some other weak D types make anti-D. Pending: D-site and weak-D molecule numbers (Number Vault).

objectives: Distinguish weak D, partial D and DEL by what changes in the RhD antigen.
Apply donor and patient RhD typing rules, including when a weak D test is required.
Use RHD genotype results to decide RhIG and blood selection for a serological weak D phenotype.

scenes.title: “Weak D positive” — so is she Rh-positive?
scenes.altText: A pregnant patient’s D typing: direct anti-D test negative; an antiglobulin (weak D) test, done anyway, is positive. Two decision cards wait: “Give RhIG?” and “Rh-positive or Rh-negative blood?”

cues.text: A pregnant patient is typed for RhD. The direct test with anti-D is negative.
Someone runs the antiglobulin weak D test anyway. It’s positive.
So does she need Rh immune globulin? And which blood should she get? It depends on what kind of D she has.

scenes.title: Normal: a D-positive red cell
scenes.altText: A schematic red cell carries many D antigens; each D antigen (a membrane protein) is drawn with a full set of epitopes, labelled a–d. Routine typing uses anti-D by direct agglutination; an antiglobulin (indirect antiglobulin, IAT) step — the “weak D test” — can detect cells with weaker D expression.

cues.text: A D-positive red cell carries many copies of the RhD protein in its membrane.
Each RhD protein shows a full set of epitopes — the small surface patches that anti-D antibodies recognise.
Routine typing mixes the cells with anti-D and looks for direct agglutination.
If that is negative or weak, an antiglobulin step — the weak D test — can pick up cells with less D on their surface.

scenes.title: What changes: weak D, partial D and DEL
scenes.altText: Three schematic cells. Weak D: fewer RhD proteins, but each has all epitopes — a quantitative change. Partial D: RhD protein with amino acid changes so some epitopes are missing (epitope gap) — a qualitative change; the person can make anti-D against the missing parts; many partial D cells still type D-positive by direct agglutination. DEL: so little D that routine typing, even the antiglobulin test, reads D-negative; only adsorption–elution or molecular testing finds it.

cues.text: Weak D: fewer RhD proteins, but each is complete. It’s a change in amount. People with the common weak D types 1, 2 and 3 have all the epitopes.

Partial D: the RhD protein is altered, so some epitopes are missing. If exposed to normal D, the person can make anti-D against the missing parts. And many partial D cells still type D-positive on direct testing.
DEL: so little D that routine typing reads D-negative — even with the antiglobulin step. Only adsorption and elution, or DNA testing, finds it.
So a typing result alone can mislead in both directions.

props.label: Typing alone can mislead both ways

scenes.title: In the lab: donors and patients follow opposite rules
scenes.altText: Two lanes. Donor lane: a weak D test is done so that weak D and partial D units are labelled D-positive and never given to D-negative recipients; DEL units still type D-negative and have caused anti-D in D-negative recipients. Patient lane (including pregnant women): a weak D test is not required — a negative direct typing is interpreted as D-negative, the safe default. If a serological weak D phenotype is found, RHD genotyping decides: weak D types 1, 2 or 3 → manage as D-positive (no RhIG, D-positive blood); other results, including partial D → manage as D-negative. Note: US monoclonal anti-D reagents for patients must not detect partial DVI on initial testing.

cues.text: For donors, the lab hunts for every trace of D. A weak D test makes sure weak D and partial D units are labelled D-positive, so they never reach a D-negative patient.
DEL is the gap: those units still type D-negative, and they have caused anti-D in D-negative recipients.
For patients, including pregnant women, the default is protective. A weak D test isn’t required; a negative direct typing is treated as D-negative.

If a weak D result does turn up, RHD genotyping settles it. Weak D types 1, 2 or 3 are managed as D-positive — no Rh immune globulin, and D-positive blood is fine. Other types, including partial D, are managed as D-negative.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Weak D test positive = Rh-positive patient” is crossed out → “Genotype first; partial D can make anti-D — manage as D-negative until resolved.” Trap card: “Recipients need a weak D test” is crossed out → “Required for donors, not recipients.” Trap card: “Types D-negative = no D at all” is crossed out → “DEL types D-negative; DEL donor units can immunize.”

cues.text: Trap one: a positive weak D test doesn’t make a patient Rh-positive. Until genotyping shows weak D type 1, 2 or 3, manage the patient as D-negative — a partial D can make anti-D.
Trap two: the weak D test is required for donors, not for transfusion recipients.
Trap three: D-negative by serology doesn’t always mean no D. DEL cells type negative, and DEL donor units have immunized D-negative recipients.

scenes.title: Donors: find it. Patients: protect them.
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Weak D is a whisper (less D, all words); partial D is a torn page (missing words); DEL is a ghost (almost nothing).” And “Donors: find every D. Patients: protect until the genotype says otherwise.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: weak D whispers — less D, but every word. Partial D is a torn page — words missing. DEL is a ghost. Donors: find every D. Patients: protect until the genotype says otherwise.

Where it breaks: which variants are common depends on ancestry; some other weak D types, such as type 4.2, have made anti-D; studies suggest Asian-type DEL patients may safely receive D-positive blood; and policies differ between countries.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Weak D = less D (types 1–3 manage as D+); partial D = missing epitopes (manage as D−)”, “Donors get a weak D test; patients default to D− until genotyped; DEL types negative”.

cues.text: Weak D types 1 to 3 are managed as D-positive, partial D as D-negative; donors are tested for weak D, patients default to D-negative until genotyped, and DEL hides as D-negative.

props.label: Weak D 1–3 → manage D+ · partial D → manage D−
Donors: weak D test · patients: D− until genotyped · DEL types D−

explanation.what: Plain language: some people have less D on their red cells, some have D with pieces missing, and some have so little that tests miss it. Scientific terms: weak D (reduced antigen density with, for types 1–3, all epitopes), partial D (amino acid substitutions with missing epitopes; can form allo-anti-D), DEL (extremely low expression, typing D-negative, detected only by adsorption–elution or molecular testing).
explanation.why: Anti-D forms against epitopes a person lacks. Weak D types 1–3 express all epitopes at lower density and have not been associated with alloimmunization; partial D lacks epitopes; DEL red cells can still immunize D-negative recipients.
explanation.measure: Donors: weak D test so weak D/partial D units are labelled D-positive. Patients and pregnant women: weak D test not required; negative direct typing interpreted as D-negative. Serological weak D → RHD genotype: weak D types 1, 2, 3 → manage as D-positive (RhIG not needed, D-positive blood acceptable); others including partial D → manage as D-negative. US monoclonal anti-D reagents for patient typing must not detect partial DVI on initial testing.
explanation.differs: Quantitative (weak D) vs qualitative (partial D) vs trace (DEL); donor rule (detect all D) vs patient rule (protect by default); serology vs RHD genotyping.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “weak D positive recipient” management, partial D making anti-D, weak D types 1/2/3 not needing RhIG, the donor weak D test, and DEL detected by adsorption–elution.

comparisons.title: Weak D vs partial D
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether all D epitopes are present — resolved by RHD genotyping.

comparisons.title: Donor vs patient D typing
comparisons.distinguisher: Donors protect recipients from D exposure; patients are protected from making anti-D.

mnemonic.text: Weak D whispers (less, but complete), partial D is a torn page (missing epitopes), DEL is a ghost. Donors: find every D; patients: protect until genotyped.
mnemonic.explanation: The metaphors map to quantitative, qualitative and trace D expression; the rule pair captures opposite donor and patient typing goals.
mnemonic.limitation: Variant frequencies depend on ancestry; some weak D types (e.g. 4.2) have made anti-D; Asian-type DEL patients may tolerate D-positive blood; national policies differ.

analogyLimitations: D tokens and epitope letters are schematic; real D sites number in the thousands.
RhCE and anti-G are not covered.
takeaway: Weak D types 1 to 3 are managed as D-positive, partial D as D-negative; donors are tested for weak D, patients default to D-negative until genotyped, and DEL hides as D-negative.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has a serological weak D phenotype. RHD genotyping shows weak D type 1. How should she be managed?

options.text: As D-positive: RhIG is not needed and D-positive blood is acceptable
options.rationale: Correct. Weak D types 1, 2 and 3 express all D epitopes and are managed as D-positive.

options.text: As D-negative: give RhIG and D-negative blood
options.rationale: Incorrect. That approach applies to partial D and other weak D types, not type 1.

options.text: Repeat serology until it turns clearly positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. Genotyping has already answered the question.
Incorrect. Adsorption–elution detects DEL, not weak D typing.

questions.stem: Why can a person with partial D form anti-D after exposure to D-positive red cells?

options.text: Their RhD protein lacks some epitopes, so they respond to the missing ones
options.rationale: Correct. Partial D is a qualitative change with missing epitopes.

options.text: They have too few D sites to tolerate normal D
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes weak D, which (for types 1–3) does not lead to anti-D.

options.text: They lack the RHD gene entirely
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the usual D-negative state, not partial D.

options.text: Partial D cells are destroyed by complement
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is unrelated to alloimmunization.

questions.stem: For which group is a weak D (antiglobulin) test required during routine RhD typing?

options.rationale: Correct. Donor units with weak or partial D must be labelled D-positive to protect D-negative recipients.
Incorrect. A weak D test is not required for recipients; a negative direct typing is treated as D-negative.
Incorrect. Standards state a weak D test is not required if the woman’s D test is negative.
Incorrect. Donor and patient rules differ.

references.citation: Sandler SG, Flegel WA, Westhoff CM, et al. It’s time to phase in RHD genotyping for patients with a serologic weak D phenotype. Transfusion. 2015;55(3):680-689.
references.usedFor: Weak D types 1, 2, 3 encode all RhD epitopes at lower density and should be managed as RhD-positive (RhIG, component selection); ~80% of serological weak D in the US mixed population are types 1–3; other weak D types (e.g. 4.2, 11, 15) have made anti-D; partial D lacks epitopes and many type D-positive by immediate spin; FDA requires patient monoclonal anti-D not to detect partial DVI on initial testing; weak D test on donors; AABB Standards: weak D test not required for women whose D test is negative; DEL types RhD-negative, detected only by adsorption–elution, implicated in alloimmunization.

references.citation: Sandler SG, Chen LN, Flegel WA. Serological weak D phenotypes: a review and guidance for interpreting the RhD blood type using the RHD genotype. Br J Haematol. 2017;179(1):10-19.
references.usedFor: Most serological weak D in Caucasians are types 1, 2 or 3 and can be managed as RhD-positive; laboratories should complete RhD testing by RHD genotyping; weak D test not required for pregnant women or recipients in the US; donors vs recipients managed differently.

references.citation: Suksard K, Luangtrakool K, Rungroung T, et al. Two cases of anti-D alloimmunization in D-negative Thai patients as a result of the Asian-type DEL on transfused red cells. Transfus Med Hemother. 2024;51(2):122-125.
references.usedFor: DEL is extremely weak D detectable only by adsorption–elution; no agglutination in the IAT, so typed D-negative; DEL donor units caused anti-D in D-negative recipients.

references.citation: Sainath PB, Ramaiyan V. Weak D phenotype in transfusion medicine and obstetrics: challenges and opportunities. World J Exp Med. 2025;15(2):102345.
references.usedFor: Weak D is a quantitative decrease; partial D loses epitopes and can alloimmunize; > 90% of weak D in a south-western German study were types 1–3; weak D types 1–3 treated as D-positive; Asian-type DEL appears D-negative but can be treated as D-positive (as recipients).

claims.text: Weak D = reduced density with all epitopes (types 1–3); partial D = missing epitopes, can make anti-D; DEL = types D-negative, adsorption–elution only.
Serological weak D in patients → RHD genotype; weak D types 1, 2, 3 managed as D-positive; others including partial D managed as D-negative.
Donors get a weak D test; patients/pregnant women do not require one; FDA partial DVI reagent requirement.
DEL donor units can immunize D-negative recipients; Asian-type DEL patients may be treated as D-positive.
D sites ~10–33 × 10³ per cell; weak D 66–5,200 molecules per cell; ~1% of D-positives type as weak D.
